coach_says: Before you push d4, count who attacks it and who defends it. Black hits d4 three times (the c6 knight, the e5 pawn and the bishop on b6) and you only defend it twice (Nf3 and the queen), so after Nxd4 Nxd4 Bxd4 you are just a pawn down. Here the quiet d3 keeps everything solid; push d4 only when you have enough support behind it.
concept: pushed a pawn it can't support
also: bishop on b6 aimed at d4

coach_says: White's d4 pawn was free: Bxd4 wins it, because the e3 pawn can't safely take back. If exd4, the e-file opens and Rxe1+ Qxe1 Qxd4+ comes with check and hits the bishop on c4 as well. b6 is a slow developing move that let White guard everything with Nc3. When a pawn looks protected, check whether the protector can actually recapture.
concept: missed a free pawn on d4

coach_says: Castling put your king on g1, exactly where the d4 knight wanted it: Ne2+ checks the king and attacks your queen on g3 at the same time, so you lose the queen. Before moving your king, look at every square an enemy knight can jump to next move. Nc3 was the move here, guarding e4 and e2 and keeping the extra piece.

Your knight on e6 was the only piece stopping mate on g7: White's queen on f7 and bishop on d4 both aim at g7, and the knight covered it. Taking the g5 pawn pulled that defender away, and Bxg7 is checkmate because your own pieces on g8 and h7 box the king in. Before you move a piece, ask what it is guarding.
also: king boxed in by own pieces

coach_says: White's e4 pawn had no defender, so Nxe4 simply won a central pawn. Taking on d4 instead gave White e5, a pawn fork hitting your bishop on d6 and knight on f6, and you only escaped because Re8 pins that pawn to the king. When the centre opens, look for an undefended pawn you can take before swapping off pawns elsewhere.

You were two pawns down and your queen on d5 was attacked twice, so this was the moment to swap queens with Qxa5 and then win back d7 with your rook: rook endings a pawn down are often drawn, especially with an active rook. After Qxd7, Re1+ forces Kh2 and then the rooks come off, leaving a queen ending against Black's passed b-pawn with your king open to checks, which is very hard to hold. When you're behind, choose which pieces to trade with care.
concept: trade queens, keep rooks, when behind
also: passed b-pawn in a queen ending

coach_says: Black's big idea in this position is Nd4, attacking your queen on f3 and threatening Nxc2+ to fork your king and rook. Nh3 puts your knight on the edge and does nothing about it, so Black plays Nd4 with gain of time and you end up pushed around. c3 first takes the d4 square away from the knight. Each move, ask what your opponent wants to do next.

Taking back on d4 left your e4 pawn with no defender, and Black took it with Nxe4. e5 first gains time: it attacks the bishop on d6 and knight on f6 together, so Black must answer that, and you can take back on d4 next move without losing a pawn. When a recapture can wait, look for a forcing move first.

You spotted the threat of Bxf7+, but Rxe3 met it and won a pawn too. The e3 pawn was attacked by your rook and your queen on g5 and defended only by the rook on e2, so after Rxe3 Rxe3 Qxe3+ you take with check. Re7 defends passively and gives White time to sort out the position. When you have to move a piece anyway, look for a capture that solves the problem.
concept: missed a free pawn on e3

coach_says: With your king still on e8, f5 opened the diagonal from h5 to e8, and Qh5+ came straight away. Ng6 just loses the knight, so the king has to walk to d7, losing castling, while White's pieces pour in on the queenside. Before moving a pawn next to an uncastled king, check which lines it opens. Developing with Nbc6 or Qc8 and getting castled was the way.
concept: opened a diagonal to the king

coach_says: When Black took back with axb6, the a-file opened and your a2 pawn was now attacked by the rook on a8. Qxb6 wins a pawn back but lets Rxa2, and that rook on your second rank, joined by Qe2, keeps attacking b2, c2 and f2. a3 keeps the pawn and keeps the rook out. When a file opens, check what's at the end of it.
also: a2 pawn left hanging on the open file

coach_says: Ra5 is a reasonable move: it puts your rook on the fifth rank where it eyes the d5 queen and stays active. The position was already difficult, and the engine's choices here are all about equal. Nothing to change.
Ne5 is a strong move: your knight lands in the centre, eyes f7 and d7, and works with the bishop on c4. d5 was just as good. Keep developing and get castled.
Bc4 is a perfectly good opening move: it develops a piece and aims at f7. Nf3 is the most common, but both are fine. Follow up by developing your knights and castling.

Your bishop on c5 was attacked by the rook on e5, and Kd6 defends it with the king, but that puts the king where Rd5+ can check it. The rook on d5 is protected by the c4 pawn, so the king must step away and Rxc5 wins the bishop anyway. The position was already very hard, but when you defend a piece with your king, check whether the attacker can give check next.
concept: defending with the king walks into check

coach_says: Qb3 is a good move: it guards c2, which the rook on c8 was attacking, and points at the d5 pawn. Qd3 was about the same. You're a pawn down, so keep your pieces defending and look for checks on Black's king.
1...c6, the Caro-Kann, is a sound and respected defence, just as good as 1...e5. Follow up with d5 to challenge White's centre.

Black was threatening Bh2+, and with your rook on f1 your king had nowhere to run: Bh2+ Kh1, then the bishop moves off with a discovered check from the rook on h8, and it's a draw by perpetual check. You're a piece up, so first give your king air: moving the f1 rook (Ra1, Rd1, Re1) frees f1 as an escape square, or g3 blocks the bishop's diagonal. Before pushing your passed pawn, make sure your king is safe from checks.
concept: king boxed in, allowing perpetual check
also: give the king an escape square

coach_says: Qg7+ looks natural but after Rg2 your queen is pinned to your king on the g-file: it can't take White's queen on h6, and it is attacked twice, so you lose it for a rook. Instead, the e5 pawn was simply hanging to Qxe5, attacked by your queen and rook with nothing defending it. Before giving check, ask whether the check can be blocked with a pin.

Taking with the b-pawn moved it off b4, and that pawn was the only thing blocking the diagonal from your opponent's queen on d6 to your knight on a3. Now Qxa3 wins the knight. Nxb5 was much better: the knight escapes from a3 with a pawn, and the black knight on a5 is still attacked by b4. When a pawn captures, check which lines it opens behind it.
concept: pawn capture opened a line to your knight
